author: Mark Atwood
text:
CORRECTION. This is our bug, not hickory's. I had it wrong, and I nearly filed a public bug report against hickory on the strength of it.

What changed my mind was writing a standalone repro in plain hickory before filing -- no workspace code -- which is the thing I should have done before concluding anything. It prints the per-record proofs:

  _25._tcp.mailly.debian.org.
     TLSA  proof=Secure
     TLSA  proof=Secure
     RRSIG proof=Secure          <- algorithm 8, DS-covered
     RRSIG proof=Indeterminate   <- algorithm 13, no DS

Both TLSA records are Secure. hickory validated the data correctly through the algorithm-8 path, which is exactly what RFC 6840 5.11 requires of a validator. There is no MUST NOT violation and nothing to report upstream.

The Indeterminate is on the algorithm-13 RRSIG -- a signature whose key the parent publishes no DS for, so hickory cannot chain that particular signature. Marking it Indeterminate is reasonable.

Our resolve() iterated lookup.answers(), which includes RRSIG records, and took the weakest proof across all of them. So that one unchainable signature dragged the whole response to Indeterminate. The comment defending the weakest-proof rule was sound for data records and wrong for signatures: an RRSIG is not part of the RRset being authenticated, it is a signature over it, and 5.11 explicitly entitles a zone to publish signatures a validator cannot chain.

Fixed by skipping RRSIG records in the status computation, extracted as answer_status() so it is testable. CNAME and DNAME are deliberately still counted -- an unauthenticated redirection must not yield authenticated data -- so the exclusion is RRSIG specifically, not 'anything that is not TLSA'.

Verified against live DNS through our own resolver: mailly.debian.org now Secure with 2 records, mx1.freebsd.org and good.dane.huque.com still Secure. Three unit tests, mutation-verified both ways: restoring RRSIG proofs fails the rollover test, and flipping weakest-to-strongest fails the injection test.

The earlier comment on this bead and the crate docs I wrote blaming hickory are both wrong and are corrected in the commit. Lesson worth keeping: I diagnosed from dig output plus our crate's verdict, which were consistent with a hickory bug and also consistent with ours. The per-record proofs told them apart, and I only looked because filing publicly made me want a clean reproduction.
